en: Sutta Nipāta 2.13 Sammāparibbājanīyasutta “I ask the Sage of abundant wisdom, [who has gone forth rightly].”
Having gone to the further shore of the three, being fully extinguished and established in self,
having gone forth from the home and cast off sensual desires—
how should such a bhikkhu rightly wander in the world?
“For whom auspicious signs have been uprooted—
(thus said the Blessed One)—
omens, dreams, and bodily marks;”
Thus, having abandoned the faults of [worldly] auspiciousness,
he should wander rightly through the world;
he should subdue passion for human beings.
Even regarding divine sensual pleasures,
a bhikkhu who has transcended existence and realized the Dhamma should wander rightly in the world.
Having cast aside slanderous speech,
a bhikkhu should abandon anger and meanness;
having utterly abandoned both compliance and hostility, he should dwell.
He should wander rightly in the world,
having abandoned both the pleasant and the unpleasant,
grasping at nothing and independent of anything whatsoever.
Freed from the fetters that bind,
he should wander rightly through the world;
he does not perceive any essence in the acquisitions (upadhi).
Having removed desire and lust for acquisitions,
independent and not led by others,
he would wander rightly in the world.
Neither in speech, nor in mind, nor in deed being at variance with others,
having rightly understood the Dhamma,
and aspiring toward the state of Nibbāna—
He would wander rightly in the world:
the bhikkhu who pays homage to one who should be honored,
and who does not become embroiled even when reviled.
Having obtained food from others, one should not become intoxicated;
thus would one wander rightly through the world,
having utterly abandoned greed and the desire for existence.
A bhikkhu who is detached from cutting and binding,
having crossed over doubt and being free from the arrow,
would wander rightly in the world.
Having recognized what is suitable for himself,
a bhikkhu should not harm anyone in the world;
having understood the Dhamma as it truly is—
He alone should wander rightly in the world,
for whom no underlying tendencies exist and whose unwholesome roots have been utterly uprooted.
Thus, free from longing and without expectations,
he should wander rightly through the world,
with the taints exhausted and conceit abandoned.
Having completely transcended every path of passion,
tamed, attained final Nibbāna, and established in himself,
he would wander rightly through the world.
The wise one, endowed with faith, learned,
and seeing the path of certainty, does not side with those who have gone astray.
Having overcome greed, hatred, and resentment, he remains steadfast.
He should wander rightly in the world:
a pure victor, with the veil removed,
a master over all phenomena, one who has reached the further shore, and is unshakable.
Skilled in the knowledge of the cessation of formations,
he would rightly wander forth in the world regarding both the past and the future.
One who has transcended the world-age, possessing wisdom that purifies through swift insight,
and who is liberated from all sense-bases—
such a one should wander rightly in the world.
Having understood the state and realized the Dhamma,
having seen the opening up of the abandonment of the taints,
and through the complete destruction of all acquisitions—
“He would indeed wander rightly in the world. “Certainly, Blessed One,
it is even so for that tamed bhikkhu who dwells in such a way.”
“Having transcended all fetters and bonds,
he would wander rightly in the world.
Thus ends the thirteenth discourse, “On Wandering Rightly.”
